questions.question: Describe how a disc brake stops a wheel, tracing the path from the pedal to the pads, and explain where Pascal's principle applies.
questions.expected_answer: A steel disc is bolted to the hub and spins with the wheel; a caliper holds a pad on each side. Pressing the pedal pushes the small master cylinder piston, raising the pressure of the brake fluid, which travels through pipes and hoses to the larger caliper pistons and pushes the pads against the disc. Friction between pads and disc slows the wheel and converts its motion into heat. Pascal's principle applies because the pressure is equal throughout the fluid, so the force at the larger caliper pistons exceeds the pedal force in the ratio of the areas and all four brakes receive the same pressure from one pedal.

questions.question: Describe how a bicycle rim brake works and identify the levers that multiply the rider's hand force.
questions.expected_answer: Squeezing the handlebar lever pulls a steel cable inside a casing; the cable swings two pivoted brake arms inward so rubber blocks pinch both sides of the wheel rim, and friction slows the wheel; a spring returns the arms when the lever is released. The handlebar lever is a second-class lever with the cable attached near the pivot and the hand far from it, multiplying the squeeze into a strong cable pull, and the brake arms are levers again, multiplying the cable pull at the blocks. The cable is in tension, the casing in compression and the arms in bending.

questions.question: Compare disc and rim brakes and evaluate a brake for fitness for purpose and safety.
questions.expected_answer: A disc brake clamps a small dedicated steel disc near the hub, needs a large hydraulic force, stays clean and dry and wears a replaceable rotor; a rim brake clamps the large wheel rim with a modest cable force, is cheap and simple, but collects water and mud, brakes poorly when wet and slowly wears the wheel. Fitness for purpose requires reliable, repeatable stopping in wet and dry conditions and full release. Safety requires that the control path cannot fail without warning: sealed fluid with no air in hydraulic systems, unfrayed cables and correctly set blocks that touch the rim and never the tyre.
